source: Schon (1983) The Reflective Practitioner
finding: Schon split professional thinking into reflection-in-action (thinking while acting) and reflection-on-action (thinking back afterwards). He set this against technical rationality.
numbers: No experiment. Case studies of architects, planners, engineers, psychotherapists, managers (secondary summary).
quote: reflecting on your actions as you are doing them
limits: Theory built from cases, not tested. The book itself was not opened; only secondary summaries.
agent_relevance: Our S5 revise step is the in-action part. A loop that acts, reads the result, and changes the next move is the core idea.

source: Schon (1983) design as conversation with the situation
finding: Design is a conversation with the situation. The designer acts as if talking to the situation, and the situation talks back. Back-talk is what a move produced beyond what was meant.
numbers: No numbers. Pattern claimed across architects, planners, engineers, psychoanalysts, scientists, managers.
limits: The Wikipedia page notes it leans on self-published and Schon-linked sources. Treat as a pointer, not proof.
agent_relevance: Back-talk maps to real output of a check (G2). The agent should listen to what its attempt returned, not to its own opinion of the attempt.

source: Schon (1983) the Quist-Petra studio case (naming, framing, moving, reflecting)
finding: From memory, not opened: in a studio session on a school on a sloping site, master Quist coached student Petra. Schon read the session as repeated cycles: name the things to attend to, frame the problem, make a move, then reflect on consequences, including unintended ones.
numbers: One session (single case). No counts reported in the book.
limits: Not opened. One case, one coach, one researcher interpreting. No inter-rater check. Hard to falsify as stated.
agent_relevance: Naming and framing map to operators that restate the problem. Moves map to attempts. Reflecting on unintended consequences is the part code can check.

source: Schon and Wiggins (1992) Kinds of seeing and their functions in designing
finding: From memory, not opened (publisher blocked fetch; abstract hidden): a seeing-moving-seeing cycle. The designer sees something in a sketch, makes a move on it, and sees again, often noticing what the move did that was not intended.
numbers: Case analysis of a design session; sample size not verified. Semantic Scholar record opened: about 958 citations, abstract withheld.
limits: Not opened. Qualitative, single case, author interpretation.
agent_relevance: A design for the loop: attempt, inspect the artefact, revise. The sketch is external memory. For the agent the artefact is code or text plus execution output.

source: Goldschmidt (1991) The dialectics of sketching
finding: From memory, not opened: designers move between seeing a sketch as something and seeing that it has some property. This back-and-forth between figural and non-figural reasoning drives new ideas.
numbers: Protocol study of architects' sketching; sample size not verified. About 1112 citations per Semantic Scholar record.
limits: Not opened; abstract hidden by the publisher. Small-sample protocol study.
agent_relevance: The loop needs an external trace to read back. For the agent: keep attempts as text it can re-inspect.

source: Suwa and Tversky (1997) What do architects and students perceive in their design sketches?
finding: Architects reported, in retrospective reports, what they read off their own freehand sketches. The study asks how designers perceptually interact with sketches and why sketches matter in early design.
numbers: Protocol analysis of retrospective reports. Participant counts not visible in the abstract I opened. About 750 citations.
quote: how they perceptually interact with and benefit from sketches
limits: Only the abstract was opened (full text blocked). Retrospective reports can be rebuilt after the fact. Expert-student differences not read.
agent_relevance: Self-reports of what was seen are post hoc. This matches our rule not to trust the model's written account of its own reasoning.

source: Valkenburg and Dorst (1998) The reflective practice of design teams
finding: From memory, not opened: design-team sessions coded with Schon's four activities (naming, framing, moving, reflecting). The activities describe team design, and teams differ in how they frame.
numbers: Small number of student design teams (N and counts not verified). About 481 citations.
limits: Not opened. Small sample, student teams, coding by the authors. Does not show reflection causes better designs.
agent_relevance: Supports reading S5 as a loop of frame, move, reflect. Gives no effect size we can reuse.

source: Suwa, Purcell and Gero (1998) Macroscopic analysis of design processes based on a scheme for coding designers' cognitive actions
finding: From memory, not opened: a four-category coding scheme (physical, perceptual, functional, conceptual actions) applied to an architect's protocol, to see how perceptual discoveries in sketches feed new requirements.
numbers: Single-designer protocol analysed in detail (not verified). About 507 citations.
limits: Not opened. One designer; scheme is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: A usable idea: log each agent step as action, perception, function or concept, to detect when back-talk led to a reframe.

source: Dorst and Dijkhuis (1995) Comparing paradigms for describing design activity
finding: From memory, not opened: the same design protocols described under a rational problem-solving paradigm and under a reflective-practice paradigm. Each captures different features.
numbers: Same protocols, two coding schemes. Counts not verified.
limits: Not opened; DOI not verified. Shows the theory is a lens, not a tested model.
agent_relevance: Suggests keeping both a plan-and-check mode and a back-talk mode in the schema.

source: Eklund, Dixon and Wegener (2023) Pre-Reflection-in-Action: Dewey, habits and Schon
finding: A recent critique says Schon's account of how acting and thinking relate needs questioning. They argue Dewey's art and habit explain how a designer can act well before reflecting.
numbers: Conceptual paper, Design Issues vol 39 no 4, pp 1-13. No data.
quote: the art-habits relationship is especially valuable for understanding design practice
limits: Only the abstract page was opened; the full text returned 403. Theory critique, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Fits the Kokotovich-style worry: much skill is habit and tacit. A prompt cannot hold habit, so expect a weaker loop than a trained designer's.

source: Critiques of Schon (Shapiro 2010; Newman; Ryan; Russell 2013)
finding: Critics say reflective models are not without problems. Dewey offered richer notions of professional growth. Students are asked to reflect without being taught how. Reflection can leave trainees with a muddled view.
numbers: No numbers. Named claims: Shapiro (2010) on Dewey; Ryan on reflecting without instruction; Russell (2013) on trainees' muddled view.
limits: Secondary source (Wikipedia). Teacher-education literature, not design cognition. Kokotovich 2015 was not found or opened; I could not verify that citation.
agent_relevance: Reflecting without a method fails. The reflect step must be a defined operator with real input, not a free 'think again'.

source: Timing critiques of reflection-in-action (Eraut and others)
finding: From memory, not opened: critics argue real-time practice leaves too little time to reflect, so reflection-in-action may be fast tacit action plus short checks.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened and not verified. Open lead for a later audit.
agent_relevance: An agent has no real-time pressure but has a call budget. Reflection must be bought with calls, so it needs a trigger (G1).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: An agent acts, gets an external signal (environment reward, unit-test result), writes a short verbal reflection on the failure, stores it in memory and tries again. A machine form of reflection-in-action.
numbers: ALFWorld (134 tasks): ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 over 12 trials, +22% absolute over baseline. HotPotQA: +20%. HumanEval Python pass@1: 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1.
limits: Needs an external signal; on ALFWorld a simple heuristic detected hallucination and inefficient planning. GPT-4 base. Quality bound by quality of the signal.
agent_relevance: Best fit for S5/O8: revise from real output and store short lessons. Matches G2.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: boundary case on MBPP Python
finding: Reflexion did not beat plain GPT-4 on MBPP Python because its own generated tests passed wrong code (false positives).
numbers: MBPP Python: Reflexion 77.1 vs GPT-4 80.1. False-positive rate of test execution: 16.3% on MBPP vs 1.4% on HumanEval. Rust HumanEval hard-50: 68.0 vs 60.0. Leetcode Hard: 15.0 vs 7.5.
limits: Self-written tests are a weak signal. When tests pass wrong code, the loop stops early.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to. A self-made test is not independent.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion ablations
finding: Removing self-generated tests hurt. Removing the written reflection step alone did not change accuracy on the hard Rust set. On HotPotQA, reflection beat plain episodic memory.
numbers: HumanEval Rust hardest 50 (GPT-4): base 0.60; no test generation 0.52; no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68. HotPotQA CoT(GT): +8% absolute from reflection over episodic memory only.
limits: Small set of 50 problems. The Rust compiler gives verbose errors, so the signal was rich.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain came from the signal (tests, compiler), not the reflection prose. Get real feedback first.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: failure analysis on ALFWorld
finding: A common baseline failure: the agent believes it holds an item, runs on, and cannot backtrack to find the mistake. ReAct-only plateaued between trials 6 and 7 with hallucinated trajectories near 22% and no recovery.
numbers: ReAct-only hallucination rate converged near 22% with no long-term recovery.
limits: Task-specific failure; Reflexion fixed it using a detection heuristic.
agent_relevance: Shows why a code-side detector for stuck states matters. Matches our impasse detector.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without oracle labels, asking a model to review and revise its own reasoning lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from using the ground-truth label to decide when to stop.
limits: Prompts taken from earlier papers; Liu et al. 2024 argue they were biased. Reasoning tasks only; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2.
agent_relevance: Core warning for O8: reflection without a real signal can hurt. Backs G1 and G2.

source: Huang et al. (2024) oracle-label effect
finding: With oracle labels the same self-correction looks like a big win. The gain disappears when the label is removed.
numbers: Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: Authors say oracle results indicate an upper bound, not true self-correction. Table read from extracted text; row alignment is my best reading.
agent_relevance: Real output acts like a mild oracle; the model's opinion does not. Supports G2.

source: Huang et al. (2024) why accuracy drops
finding: The model changes correct answers to wrong ones more often than it fixes wrong ones. It cannot judge its own reasoning.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time. On CSQA GPT-3.5 changes answers far more, since wrong options look relevant.
limits: GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo kept answers more often, maybe from higher confidence.
agent_relevance: Gate reflection by a signal (G1). Default is to keep the first answer.

source: Huang et al. (2024) multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: At matched number of responses, majority vote beat multi-agent debate on GSM8K.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: single 76.7; debate round 1 (6 responses) 83.2 vs vote of 6: 85.3; debate round 2 (9) 83.0 vs vote of 9: 88.2.
limits: One benchmark, one model. Row pairing inferred from the extracted table.
agent_relevance: Adds to G4: a second voice from the same model adds little. Prefer code-checked selection.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Self-correction split into finding the mistake and fixing it. Models are poor at finding it; given the true location, they fix well. Back-talk must be located by something other than the model.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces from PaLM 2 with first-error step labeled. Best model GPT-4 reaches 52.87 overall accuracy at finding the error (step-level prompting). Backtracking with true location, gain on wrong traces: +23.53 word sorting, +43.92 shuffled objects, +36.86 logical deduction, +18.04 arithmetic, +18.06 Dyck.
limits: Five tasks. Traces from one generator (PaLM 2). A true location is not available in practice.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: code locates the failing step, the model fixes it. Most useful LLM result for S5.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) cost of backtracking and random-location control
finding: Backtracking on originally correct traces loses some accuracy, but gains on wrong traces are larger. A random location gives smaller gains than the true one.
numbers: Losses on correct traces with true location: -11.11, -6.67, -11.43, 0.00, -6.82 (same task order). Random location gains on wrong traces: +11.76, +20.39, +21.57, +10.59, +5.16. 15% of traces had correct answers, 85% incorrect. Mean trace length 5.0 to 24.5 steps.
limits: With 85% wrong traces there is much to gain; on easier mixes the net effect would shrink.
agent_relevance: Revise only when failure is likely (G1). A random redo helps on wrong traces, so part of the gain is resampling.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: One model drafts, gives feedback on its draft and refines it. Large gains on style and constraint tasks, small on math.
numbers: Seven tasks; about 20% absolute average gain claimed. Code optimization GPT-4: 27.3 to 36.0. Constrained generation: 29.0 to 49.7 over 3 iterations. Math: ChatGPT feedback said everything looks good in 94% of cases; with an external error detector gains exceed 5%.
limits: Tasks with checkable or stylistic criteria. Vicuna-13B could not follow the feedback prompts.
agent_relevance: Reflection helps where the critic can see the flaw. Use it for tasks with a checkable property.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Verification through tools (search, code interpreter) before revision. Removing the tool lowers results.
numbers: ChatGPT free-form QA, first score column: CRITIC 50.0 vs CRITIC without tool 42.0 (ReAct 47.6). Other columns keep the order (64.9 vs 58.3). Tasks: QA, math program synthesis, toxicity.
limits: Column labels in the extracted table were unclear, so only the ordering is firm.
agent_relevance: External checks do the work. Back-talk from the world beats back-talk from the model's opinion.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works with reliable external feedback. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Qualitative survey. Tasks where intrinsic correction works: decomposable responses (e.g. CoVe lists) and verifiable tasks (e.g. constrained generation).
limits: Review of published work. Many studies used oracle information or weak initial prompts.
agent_relevance: Rule: reflect with external signal or on decomposable tasks, else keep the first answer.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) feedback generation is the bottleneck
finding: Feedback generation is the bottleneck. Using external tools or knowledge such as code interpreters and search engines is promising.
numbers: No single number.
limits: Survey ends around mid-2024.
agent_relevance: Our program, not the model, should generate the feedback (checks, counts, test output).

source: Kumar et al. (2024) SCoRe: training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning
finding: Training, not prompting, can create real self-correction. Base models get worse on a second try; multi-turn RL gives the first clearly positive gain.
numbers: MATH, Gemini 1.5 Flash: base second-try change -11.2 points; Self-Refine about -1.0; SCoRe +4.4 intrinsic gain (+15.6 over base). HumanEval: SCoRe +12.2 gain, 9 points above the base.
limits: Needs RL on a model. We do not train. Offline SFT variants collapsed to minimal edits.
agent_relevance: The weakness is trainable, so prompting alone has a ceiling. Confirms we need external signals.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Intrinsic self-correction is not a mirage: zero temperature and fair prompts
finding: Counter-evidence to Huang et al.: with zero temperature and neutral prompts, intrinsic correction gives small gains. Wording like find problems pushes the model to change right answers.
numbers: Four models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral, Llama 3.1), six datasets. Fair prompts improve averages (p<0.05 and p<0.003). CSQA before correction: GPT-3.5 75.92, GPT-4 84.11.
limits: Gains small; per-dataset gains not recorded here. Four models and six datasets only.
agent_relevance: Word the reflect step neutrally and allow no change (G1).

source: Stechly, Valmeekam and Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 doesn't know it's wrong
finding: From memory, not opened: self-critique of GPT-4 on graph colouring lowered accuracy, while critique from an external sound verifier raised it.
numbers: Numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened; arXiv id unverified. Planning-style task.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Huang: an external verifier works, self-critique does not.

source: Gap: LLM studies that test Schon directly
finding: I found no paper that runs an LLM agent against Schon's own predictions (naming, framing, back-talk) with measured results. Reflexion-type work is the closest functional match.
numbers: Zero direct studies found. The search budget was exhausted; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate limits blocked a fuller scan.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search. Retry when budgets reset.
agent_relevance: Treat Schon as design inspiration and rely on the self-correction literature for numbers.

source: Kokotovich critique (reflection leans on tacit experience)
finding: The task brief says Kokotovich (2015) argues the theory leans on tacit experience and narrows what is considered. I could not find or open this paper to check it.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Unverified citation. A Kokotovich 2008 Design Studies paper exists but is a different topic.
agent_relevance: If true, the schema should widen the search when stuck, but only on a signal (G1).
